funFacts: Its acorns wear a shaggy, fringed cap — like a tiny furry hat.
Bur oaks have thick, corky bark that helps them survive prairie fires.
Some bur oaks in the Chicago area are over 200 years old and were already big trees before Chicago was a city.
whoLivesHere: Squirrels, blue jays, and deer all compete for its big acorns. Dozens of moth and butterfly caterpillars feed only on oak leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Bur oak acorns have a shaggy fringed cap; white oak acorns have a smooth bowl-shaped cap.
Bur oak leaves have rounded lobes; red oak leaves have sharp, pointed lobes.

winterClues: Thick, deeply furrowed gray-brown bark and stout branches that spread out horizontally like open arms.

funFacts: New leaves unfurl pinkish-red before turning dark green for the summer.
It's one of the faster-growing oaks, so it doesn't take as long to get big.
Its sharp-pointed leaf lobes are the easiest way to tell it apart from round-lobed oaks.
whoLivesHere: Acorns feed turkeys, woodpeckers, and raccoons. Caterpillars of many moths rely on its leaves.

lookalikes.howToTell: Red oak lobes end in sharp points; bur oak lobes are rounded.

winterClues: Dark gray bark with flat-topped ridges that can look almost like shiny ski trails running up the trunk.

funFacts: White oak is the official state tree of Illinois.
It can live more than 200 years — some White Oaks alive today sprouted before the Civil War.
Its acorns have a smooth, bowl-shaped cap and are less bitter than most oaks'.
whoLivesHere: Supports more kinds of moths, butterflies, and songbirds than almost any other tree in the Midwest.

lookalikes.howToTell: White oak's acorn cap is smooth and bowl-shaped; bur oak's is shaggy and fringed.

winterClues: Light gray, flaky bark broken into rectangular blocks, and wide horizontal branches.

funFacts: Flip a leaf over — the underside is silvery white, which is how it got its name.
It grows fast and is often found along creeks and rivers.
Its branches can snap in high wind or ice storms, so arborists prune it carefully.
whoLivesHere: Squirrels eat its winged seeds, and its early spring flowers are an important first meal for bees.

lookalikes.howToTell: Silver maple leaves have deep, narrow notches between lobes and silvery undersides; sugar maple leaves are more evenly lobed and green underneath.

winterClues: Gray bark that peels in long, shaggy strips on older trunks, with branches that often droop and curve upward at the tips.

funFacts: This is the tree maple syrup comes from — its sap runs sweet in late winter.
Its five-lobed leaf is famous as the maple leaf on Canada's flag.
It's one of the showiest trees for fall color in the Chicago area.
whoLivesHere: Squirrels and chipmunks eat its seeds; its dense canopy is a favorite nesting spot for songbirds.

lookalikes.howToTell: Sugar maple's lobes are more rounded with U-shaped notches; silver maple's notches cut in deep and narrow.

winterClues: Gray, furrowed bark in long vertical plates, with opposite branching (twigs grow in pairs across from each other).

funFacts: It was brought over from Europe and Asia and planted along streets everywhere.
Snap its leaf stem — milky white sap drips out, which no native maple does.
It spreads so many seeds that it crowds out native wildflowers in wooded areas.
whoLivesHere: Its dense shade and heavy seed crop actually make it harder for native plants to grow underneath it.

lookalikes.howToTell: Norway maple's leaf stem oozes milky sap when snapped; sugar maple's sap is clear.

winterClues: Grayish-black bark with a fine, crisscross pattern, and buds that are noticeably plump and rounded.
troubleTree: Planted widely as a street tree, but it spreads aggressively into woods and can crowd out native trees.

funFacts: Its leaves are made of 15-30 tiny leaflets, so one 'leaf' looks like a feather.
Wild honeylocusts grow long, sharp thorns, but most planted in cities are a thornless variety.
Its light, lacy shade lets grass grow even underneath the tree.
whoLivesHere: Its long seed pods feed deer and livestock; the dappled shade is gentle enough for understory plants to thrive.

lookalikes.howToTell: Honeylocust leaflets are small and smooth-edged; black walnut leaflets are larger and slightly toothed, with a spicy smell when crushed.

winterClues: Dark, rough bark with long vertical ridges; thornless cultivars have smooth twigs, while wild trees show clusters of sharp thorns on the trunk.

funFacts: In early summer, its seeds drift through the air on little tufts of cotton, like a snow flurry.
It's one of the fastest-growing trees in North America.
Its triangle-shaped leaves have a flat leaf stem that makes them flutter noisily in the wind.
whoLivesHere: Bald eagles and great blue herons often nest in its tall branches near rivers.
winterClues: Thick, ash-gray bark with deep furrows; look for it along rivers and low, wet ground.

funFacts: Its bark peels away in long, curling plates, making the whole trunk look shaggy.
It grows tasty nuts inside a thick green husk that splits open in fall.
It's a slow grower, but can live 200 years or more.
whoLivesHere: Squirrels bury its nuts to eat later, and bats sometimes roost behind its loose, peeling bark.
winterClues: Long strips of bark curl outward from the trunk, as if the tree is wearing a shaggy gray coat.

funFacts: Its bark peels off in patches, revealing bright white or pale green bark underneath.
It's one of the biggest native trees in the Chicago region — some grow over 100 feet tall.
Its round, dangling seed balls stay on the tree through winter.
whoLivesHere: Its hollow trunks often shelter owls, raccoons, and squirrels.
winterClues: Patchy white, gray, and brown bark that looks almost like camouflage, easiest to spot in winter.

funFacts: Ginkgo trees have barely changed in over 200 million years — dinosaurs saw leaves just like these.
Its fan-shaped leaves all turn gold at once and can drop in a single day.
Only male ginkgos are usually planted in cities, because female trees drop smelly fruit.
whoLivesHere: Very few local insects eat ginkgo leaves, since the tree is originally from Asia, not Chicago.
winterClues: Grayish bark with shallow ridges and short, stubby side branches called spur shoots.

funFacts: Crush its leaves and you'll smell a spicy, almost citrusy scent.
Its roots release a chemical that stops some other plants from growing nearby.
The hard-shelled nuts inside green husks are a favorite target for squirrels.
whoLivesHere: Squirrels bury and hoard its nuts all over the neighborhood, which is how new walnut trees often sprout.

lookalikes.howToTell: Black walnut leaflets are larger with slightly toothed edges and a spicy smell; honeylocust leaflets are smaller and smooth-edged.

winterClues: Dark, deeply furrowed bark in a diamond pattern, and branch tips with a chambered (segmented) pith inside twigs.

funFacts: In early spring, its bare branches burst into clusters of pink-magenta flowers before any leaves appear.
Its leaves are heart-shaped, which makes it one of the easiest trees to recognize.
It naturally grows at the edges of forests, which is why it does fine with some shade in a yard.
whoLivesHere: Its early flowers are an important first source of nectar for bees each spring.
winterClues: Smooth gray bark that turns reddish and scaly with age, and flattened, dark seed pods that hang on through winter.

funFacts: It was planted all over the country because it blooms with a huge burst of white flowers every spring.
The flowers smell bad to a lot of people — some say like old socks or fish.
It was originally bred to be seedless, but different varieties cross-pollinated and now it spreads on its own.
whoLivesHere: It spreads so fast into wild areas that it crowds out native trees and shrubs, so it isn't actually great for local wildlife.
winterClues: Smooth gray bark and a tight, symmetrical branch shape; wild offspring growing outside yards often have sharp thorns.
troubleTree: Illinois is banning the sale of Callery pear (including the 'Bradford' pear) starting January 1, 2028, because it spreads aggressively into wild areas and crowds out native plants.

funFacts: Its branches spread out and arch over like a graceful fountain — this is called a 'vase shape.'
A tiny beetle spreads a disease called Dutch elm disease, which killed millions of American elms starting in the 1950s.
New disease-resistant varieties like 'Princeton' and 'Valley Forge' are being replanted on city streets today.
whoLivesHere: Its seeds feed songbirds and squirrels in spring, and its broad canopy once shaded entire city blocks in old neighborhoods.
winterClues: Gray, deeply furrowed bark and a vase-shaped silhouette — the trunk splits into wide arching branches instead of growing straight up.

funFacts: It's one of the most widely spread trees in eastern North America — and the first to blaze red in fall.
Even its flowers, seeds, and new twigs are reddish, not just its fall leaves.
Its shallow roots can heave up nearby sidewalks, so it's often planted a little further back from pavement.
whoLivesHere: Its early red flowers are one of the first spring nectar sources for bees, and its seeds feed squirrels and chipmunks.

lookalikes.howToTell: Red maple's lobes are separated by sharp V-shaped notches; sugar maple's notches are more rounded and U-shaped.

winterClues: Smooth gray bark when young, turning dark and plated with age; reddish twigs and flower buds visible all winter.

funFacts: It's a close cousin of sugar maple — so close that some scientists consider it the same species.
Its leaves often droop slightly at the edges, giving them a relaxed, slightly wilted look even when healthy.
Like sugar maple, its sap can be tapped to make maple syrup.
whoLivesHere: Its dense, rounded crown shelters nesting songbirds, and its seeds feed squirrels through fall.

lookalikes.howToTell: Black maple leaves often droop at the edges and have fewer, shallower lobes than sugar maple.

winterClues: Dark, furrowed bark similar to sugar maple, with a dense, rounded winter silhouette.

funFacts: It's originally from Japan, Korea, and China, and was brought to the US as a prized ornamental yard tree.
Its leaves are deeply cut into delicate, lacy points — there are over 1,000 known varieties.
Unlike the towering street and park trees on this list, it's usually planted small and close to a house or garden path.
whoLivesHere: It's mostly grown for looks rather than wildlife value, but its dense branching still offers cover for small birds.
winterClues: Thin, often reddish young branches with a delicate, layered branching pattern, usually on a small, ornamental-sized tree.

funFacts: Unlike most oaks, its leaf edges are wavy instead of deeply lobed.
Flip a leaf over — the underside is silvery-white, very different from its dark green top.
It's tough enough to handle both flooding and city street conditions, which is why parks plant it near rivers.
whoLivesHere: Its acorns feed game birds and small mammals, and it's especially valuable along floodplains like the one at Horner Park.

lookalikes.howToTell: Swamp white oak leaves have wavy edges rather than the deep rounded lobes of a bur oak.

winterClues: Peeling, curling bark — especially noticeable on younger trees — often found growing near rivers and low ground.

funFacts: Its bark peels and curls in dramatic cinnamon-and-pink strips — the easiest way to spot it from far away.
It's naturally resistant to the beetle that kills most other birches, so it stays healthy in cities.
It grows fast and loves wet ground, which is why you'll find it lining river paths.
whoLivesHere: Its curling bark gives insects a place to hide, which in turn brings in woodpeckers and nuthatches looking for a meal.
winterClues: Salmon-pink to reddish-brown bark that peels away in curling, papery layers — unmistakable even bare in winter.

funFacts: Its long, drooping branches hang right down over the water, like it's dangling its fingers in the river.
It's one of the fastest-growing native trees, but it only lives about 40-50 years.
Its wood is so bendy and brittle that its branches snap easily — don't climb this one!
whoLivesHere: Its branches shade the river for fish, and beavers and muskrats often gnaw on its bark and twigs.
winterClues: Gray-brown bark broken into shaggy furrowed plates, with long drooping branches that often trail into the water.

funFacts: It's a conifer that does something almost no other conifer does — it drops all its needles every fall.
Its natural home is the swampy southern US, but it handles Chicago winters just fine when planted here.
In really wet ground, it sometimes grows odd woody knobs called 'knees' poking up around its base.
whoLivesHere: Its soft, feathery needles and open canopy let light reach the ground below, and birds nest in its tall, straight branches.
winterClues: A tall, straight conifer that's completely bare of needles in winter — unlike pines and spruces nearby.

funFacts: Its bark is covered in strange, warty, cork-like ridges — once you've felt it, you'll never forget it.
Its small purple berries stay on the tree all winter, which makes it a favorite snack stop for birds.
It's incredibly tough and handles tricky city conditions — salt, drought, bad soil — better than most trees.
whoLivesHere: Its persistent winter berries feed robins, cedar waxwings, and other birds when little else is available.

lookalikes.howToTell: Hackberry bark is warty and corky instead of ridged like elm, and its leaves are more evenly toothed along the edge.

winterClues: Gray bark covered in distinctive warty, cork-like ridges and bumps — easy to identify by touch alone.

funFacts: Its heart-shaped leaves are some of the biggest of any tree on this list — almost as big as your face.
It's nicknamed the 'cigar tree' because of its long, skinny, hanging seed pods.
In late spring it bursts into huge clusters of white, orchid-like flowers.
whoLivesHere: Its flowers attract bees and hummingbirds, and the catalpa sphinx moth caterpillar feeds only on its leaves.
winterClues: Thick, blunt twigs and long, skinny, cigar-shaped seed pods that often hang on well into winter.

funFacts: Its leaves are made of about 70 tiny leaflets — one of the biggest compound leaves of any tree here.
Pioneers once roasted its seeds as a coffee substitute — though the raw seeds are toxic, so don't try it yourself!
Its leaves don't even appear until late May, so in spring it looks bare long after other trees have leafed out.
whoLivesHere: Its thick, leathery seed pods are too tough for most animals to eat, so they often sit on the ground through winter.
winterClues: Thick, blunt, almost prehistoric-looking twigs with no small side branches, and large woody pods on the ground nearby.

funFacts: It grows long, sharp thorns up to 2 inches — watch your fingers!
Its leaves and branches feel slightly fuzzy or 'downy' to the touch, which is how it got its name.
Its bright red, apple-like fruits called pomes stay on the tree well into fall, feeding birds.
whoLivesHere: Its thorny branches make a safe nesting spot for small birds that predators can't easily reach.
winterClues: Twisted, thorny branches (thorns 1-2 inches long) and small round fruits that may still cling on into winter.

funFacts: It's also called 'Juneberry' because its sweet, blueberry-like fruit ripens in June.
It's one of the first trees to bloom in spring, covered in clouds of white flowers.
Its smooth, silvery-gray bark looks a little like beech bark.
whoLivesHere: Its June berries are one of the first ripe fruits of the year for birds, and its early flowers feed hungry spring bees.
winterClues: Smooth, silvery-gray bark with faint vertical streaks, on a small, multi-stemmed understory tree.

funFacts: It's a giant version of the lilac bushes in your yard — but it grows as a real tree, not a shrub.
In June it's covered in huge, fragrant clusters of creamy white flowers, much later than other lilacs.
Its reddish-brown bark has little horizontal slits, just like a cherry tree's bark.
whoLivesHere: Its late, nectar-rich flowers are an important early-summer stop for bees and butterflies.
winterClues: Reddish-brown bark marked with short horizontal lines, resembling a cherry tree's trunk.
